conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor on call. I understand you came in with left upper abdominal pain near your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started about two days ago. It’s this sharp pain on the left side, right around the tube. I’ve been able to do my tube feeds and eat a little, but today I just don’t want to eat because it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills? Any diarrhea or constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. No diarrhea. I don’t think I’m constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about vomiting—has your cyclic vomiting been acting up more than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had nausea and some vomiting like I usually do, but the pain is what’s different. I’m worried the tube moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a reasonable concern. On exam your belly is soft, but you’re tender right near the tube site. We’ll check labs and have Interventional Radiology evaluate the tube position and likely exchange it if it’s not sitting right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Like could it be leaking inside?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If a tube is out of position it can cause pain and irritation, and rarely leakage. Right now you look stable—no fever, your abdomen isn’t rigid, and your vitals are okay. The safest next step is imaging with contrast through the tube in IR and replacing it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: While we’re getting things arranged, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and give you medication for nausea and pain. We’ll also continue your stomach-protecting medicines like pantoprazole and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I still use the tube tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, let’s hold tube feeds until IR checks it. Small sips by mouth are okay if you can tolerate them, but we’ll prioritize keeping you comfortable and not worsening nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your morning labs are back—your electrolytes and kidney function look normal, and your white blood cell count is not elevated, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing in the labs suggests infection right now. The pain seems localized to the tube area, so tube position and local irritation are still the top concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will they fix the tube? It really hurts when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: IR is planning to take you today. They’ll inject contrast through the tube under X-ray to see where it sits, and then exchange it over a wire through the same tract if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be put to sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually it’s moderate sedation—medication through the IV to make you sleepy and comfortable, plus numbing medicine at the skin. You’ll be monitored the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go down, any new symptoms—worsening vomiting, chest pain, shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the same nausea and the pain at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: IR is ready for you. After the exchange, we’ll reassess your pain and decide when to restart your home meds and oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from IR. They exchanged the gastrostomy tube through the same tract and confirmed it’s positioned in the gastric pouch area. They also treated some irritated tissue at the skin entry site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember them saying something about burning the tissue. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—when there’s overgrowth of granulation tissue at the skin, they can apply silver nitrate to reduce it. It can sting briefly, but it helps with irritation and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is better than before, but it’s still sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness is expected for a few days after an exchange. We’ll use oral pain medicine as needed, and we can add a lidocaine patch near the site to help with localized pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go back to tube feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk about that. The tube is currently in the gastric pouch, which is connected up to your esophagus. Feeding into that area may not help the way feeding into the excluded stomach would, especially with cyclic vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube isn’t doing what it’s supposed to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may not be providing the benefit we want for nutrition if it’s effectively feeding the same pathway that triggers nausea and vomiting. That’s why we want to follow up with an endoscopy to better map your anatomy and make a longer-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you saying I should have it removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that option because if it’s not useful, keeping it can mean ongoing site discomfort and care needs. But it’s your decision. If you’re not ready to remove it now, we can leave it in place and reassess after the endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want it removed today. I’m scared I’ll end up unable to eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll defer removal. For now, we’ll focus on controlling pain and nausea and making sure you can take nutrition by mouth safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with sips of liquids or small amounts by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve kept down some liquids. I’m still nauseated but not throwing up right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll restart your home medications tonight—pantoprazole twice daily and sucralfate four times daily are important given your history of ulcers. We’ll also continue ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My antidepressant and anxiety meds—will I get those too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your citalopram, lorazepam, and quetiapine as you take them at home. We also have nortriptyline on your list; we’ll keep it at the dose you’ve been using.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning check-in. How was the night? Any vomiting? How’s the tube site pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight. The site is sore but not like yesterday. I can walk around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your repeat labs remain stable. Since you’re tolerating oral intake, we can plan for discharge later today if pain stays controlled on oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I do with the tube at home if I’m not using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s not in use, you can cap the outside opening and secure the tube to your abdomen with tape so it doesn’t tug. Check the site daily for redness, swelling, warmth, bad odor, or yellow/bloody drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—wash gently with warm soapy water and keep it clean and dry afterward. Avoid baths, swimming, or hot tubs—don’t submerge the site in water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about malnutrition. That’s what they keep telling me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The concern is that with persistent vomiting and limited intake after bariatric surgery, it’s easy to fall behind on calories and protein. Right now you’re able to take some nutrition by mouth, and we’re keeping you on vitamins and iron. The endoscopy follow-up will help us decide the best long-term way to support nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s review your discharge medications. You’ll continue pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day and sucralfate 1 gram four times a day. You’ll also continue your multivitamin, vitamin D, and iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For the tube site pain, you’ll have a lidocaine patch to place near the site daily, and an oxycodone-acetaminophen liquid to use only as needed. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m afraid the pain meds will make me nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen. Use the smallest amount you need, and rely on the lidocaine patch and non-medication measures when possible. If you do need the liquid pain medicine, take it with what you can tolerate by mouth and use ondansetron as prescribed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call if you have severe or worsening pain, fever over 101.5, increasing redness or drainage at the site, or if you’re vomiting and can’t keep down fluids or medications. Also come in for signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing, very dry mouth, or a fast heartbeat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the plan is an endoscopy soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—follow up with the bariatric surgery team in early follow-up for an endoscopy to better delineate your anatomy and decide what to do about the gastrostomy tube and nutrition plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: you’re walking independently, your pain is controlled with oral meds, and you’re tolerating oral nutrition. Are you comfortable going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still nervous, but I feel better than when I came in. I’ll watch the site and follow up.
